desc:
Given two integer arrays a and b, return the values that occur in both arrays. Each common value must be reported exactly once, no matter how many copies of it the arrays contain, and the result must be sorted in increasing order.

For example, a = [4, 9, 5, 9] and b = [9, 4, 9, 8, 4] give [4, 9]. If there is no common value, return an empty array.
constraints: The result is sorted ascending and has no repeated values
hints: Checking every pair of elements works but is O(n · m). Which structure answers 'is this value in the other array?' in O(1)?
Put one array into a hash set. Then scan the other array and keep the values found in the set.
Repeats must disappear, so collect the matches in a set as well (or intersect two sets directly) and sort the final result.
editorial: Convert both arrays to sets: this removes repeats immediately and gives O(1) membership tests. The set intersection set(a) & set(b) contains exactly the values present in both arrays. Sorting that set produces the required output.

Building the sets takes O(n + m) and sorting the result O(k log k) where k is the number of common values. If both inputs were already sorted, a two-pointer merge would find the common values without extra memory, but for unsorted input the hash set is the natural choice. Compare with the multiplicity-preserving variant, where a counter is needed instead of a set.
solution:
def intersectionUnique(a, b):
    return sorted(set(a) & set(b))
